title: Sensation & perception
examples: What is the difference between sensation and perception?
How does my expectation affect what I see?
Can you give an example of a perceptual set in action?

explain.say: Today we are looking at how we sense and then how we perceive things.
The first idea is understanding sensory thresholds in our senses.
A concrete example involves the absolute threshold for light.
Next we explore the concept of the difference threshold, or JND.
Our third point is the perceptual set, which is key to interpretation.
For an everyday example, think about reading a street sign.

faq.q: What is the difference between sensation and perception?
faq.a: Sensation is the raw data coming from your sensory organs. Perception is your brain making sense of that raw data.
asks: How do I process sensory information?
Is sensation just input, and perception is output?

faq.a: It is the minimum amount of a stimulus that you can detect five times out of ten. This is the lowest level needed for detection.
asks: What is the lowest level I can sense?
Does the absolute threshold change for different senses?

faq.a: The JND is the smallest difference between two stimuli that you can just barely notice. It shows how sensitive you are to change.
asks: What is the measurable difference threshold?
Is JND related to how much I already know?

faq.a: It means your expectations or context influence how you interpret what you are sensing. You see what you expect to see.
asks: Does what I expect to see change my vision?
Can my mood affect my perception?

faq.q: Are thresholds the same for all senses?
faq.a: No, the thresholds are different for each sense, like sight, hearing, and touch. Each sense has its own measurable limits.
asks: Does sight have a different threshold than hearing?
Are there universal thresholds for all humans?

facts: Sensation is the process of receiving stimuli through the senses.
The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus required for detection.
The difference threshold, or JND, is the smallest noticeable change.
A perceptual set means your prior knowledge guides your interpretation of input.

quiz.say: A student can only detect a very faint smell when it is stronger than a certain level. This level represents the:
quiz.why: The absolute threshold is the minimum stimulus needed for any detection.

wrong.0: This is getting used to a constant stimulus, not detecting the first one.
wrong.2: This measures change, not the initial detection level.
wrong.3: This relates to expectation, not physical limits.

quiz.say: If you know a certain sound is coming, you might hear it even if it is slightly quieter than usual. This is an example of:
quiz.why: Your expectation about the sound makes you interpret weaker signals as present.

wrong.1: This would suggest the sound is above the minimum detectable level.
wrong.2: This measures the smallest change you notice, not the presence itself.
wrong.3: This would mean you stopped noticing the sound altogether.

quiz.say: A scientist needs to find the weakest light source that a person can just barely see. Which concept is being tested?
quiz.why: The weakest detectable stimulus is the definition of the absolute threshold.

wrong.0: This would involve asking the person what they expect to see.
wrong.1: This is too vague; the specific term is absolute threshold.
wrong.3: This would require comparing two different light sources.
